A tribe of Indians who, when first known, lived on the Ottawa River. Most of them subsequently migrated to the southwestern shore of Lake Superior.

Any carnivorous animal of the genus Lutra, and related genera. Several species are described. They have large, flattish heads, short ears, and webbed toes. They are aquatic, and feed on fish. Their fur is soft and valuable. The common otter of Europe is Lutra vulgaris; the American otter is L. Canadensis; other species inhabit South America and Asia.

The larva of the ghost moth. It is very injurious to hop vines. Otter hound, Otter dog (Zoöl.), a small breed of hounds, used in England for hunting otters.  -- Otter sheep. See Ancon sheep, under Ancon.  -- Otter shell (Zoöl.), very large bivalve mollusk (Schizothærus Nuttallii) found on the northwest coast of America. It is excellent food, and is extensively used by the Indians.  -- Sea otter. (Zoöl.) See in the Vocabulary.
A corruption of Annotto.
See Attar.

A four-stroke cycle for internal-combustion engines consisting of the following operations: First stroke, suction into cylinder of explosive charge, as of gas and air; second stroke, compression, ignition, and explosion of this charge; third stroke (the working stroke), expansion of the gases; fourth stroke, expulsion of the products of combustion from the cylinder. This is the cycle invented by Beau de Rochas in 1862 and applied by Dr. Otto in 1877 in the Otto-Crossley gas engine, the first commercially successful internal- combustion engine made.
An engine using the Otto cycle.
Of or pertaining to the Turks; as, the Ottoman power or empire.
A Turk.
A stuffed seat without a back, originally used in Turkey.
An Ottoman. [R.] Shak.
A micaceous mineral occurring in small scales. It is characteristic of certain crystalline schists.
Any South American monkey of the genus Brachyurus, especially B. ouakari.

A small landlocked variety of the Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar ounaniche) of Lake St. John, Canada, and neighboring waters, noted for its vigor and activity, and habit of leaping from the water when hooked.
The wanderoo.
A Brazilian monkey of the genus Mycetes.

A dungeon with an opening only at the top, found in some old castles and other strongholds, into which persons condemned to perpetual imprisonment, or to perish secretly, were thrust, or lured to fall. Sudden in the sun An oubliette winks. Where is he Gone. Mrs. Browning.
A socket or bezel holding a precious stone; hence, a jewel or ornament worn on the person. A precious stone in a rich ouche. Sir T. Elyot. Your brooches, pearls, and ouches. Shak.
Own. [Obs.] Chaucer.
See Aught.

synonyms: Ought, Should. Both words imply obligation, but ought is the stronger. Should may imply merely an obligation of propriety, expendiency, etc.; ought denotes an obligation of duty.
definitions: Was or were under obligation to pay; owed. [Obs.] This due obedience which they ought to the king. Tyndale. The love and duty I long have ought you. Spelman. [He] said . . . you ought him a thousand pound. Shak.
Owned; possessed. [Obs.] The knight the which that castle ought. Spenser.
To be bound in duty or by moral obligation. We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak. Rom. xv. 1.

To be necessary, fit, becoming, or expedient; to behoove; -- in this sense formerly sometimes used impersonally or without a subject expressed. "Well ought us work." Chaucer. To speak of this as it ought, would ask a volume. Milton. Ought not Christ to have suffered these things Luke xxiv. 26.
The state of being as a thing ought to be; rightness. [R.] N. W. Taylor.
Anywhere; somewhere. See Owher. [Obs.]
See Wistit.
An awl. [Obs.] Chaucer.
An owl. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Same as Eulachon.
A weight, the sixteenth part of a pound avoirdupois, and containing 437
The twelfth part of a troy pound.
Fig.: A small portion; a bit. [Obs.] By ounces hung his locks that he had. Chaucer. Fluid ounce. See under Fluid, n.

A feline quadruped (Felis irbis, or uncia) resembling the leopard in size, and somewhat in color, but it has longer and thicker fur, which forms a short mane on the back. The ounce is pale yellowish gray, with irregular dark spots on the neck and limbs, and dark rings on the body. It inhabits the lofty mountain ranges of Asia. Called also once.
Wavy; waving [Obs.] "Owndie hair." Chaucer.
Waving. [Obs.] Ounding, paling, winding, or bending . . . of cloth. Chaucer.
A fairy; a goblin; an elf. [Obs.] "Like urchins, ouphes, and fairies." Shak.
Elfish. [Obs.]
Of or pertaining to us; belonging to us; as, our country; our rights; our troops; our endeavors. See I. The Lord is our defense. Ps. lxxxix. 18.
See -or.
The orang-outang.
See Orang-outang.
See Uranographist.
See Uranography.
A small, graceful, and swift African antelope, allied to the klipspringer.
Uric.
See Urology.
Ourology.
See Note under Our.

; sing. Ourself (we; also, alone in the predicate, in the nominative or the objective case. We ourselves might distinctly number in words a great deal further then we usually do. Locke. Safe in ourselves, while on ourselves we stand. Dryden.

An adjective suffix meaning full of, abounding in, having, possessing the qualities of, like; as in gracious, abounding in grace; arduous, full of ardor; bulbous, having bulbs, bulblike; riotous, poisonous, piteous, joyous, etc.

A suffix denoting that the element indicated by the name bearing it, has a valence lower than that denoted by the termination -ic; as, nitrous, sulphurous, etc., as contrasted with nitric, sulphuric, etc.
See Ooze. [Obs.]

One of several species of European thrushes, especially the blackbird (Merula merula, or Turdus merula), and the mountain or ring ousel (Turdus torquatus). [Written also ouzel.] Rock ousel (Zoöl.), the ring ousel.  -- Water ousel (Zoöl.), the European dipper (Cinclus aquaticus), and the American dipper (C. Mexicanus).
See Oast.
To take away; to remove. Multiplication of actions upon the case were rare, formerly, and thereby wager of law ousted. Sir M. Hale.
To eject; to turn out. Blackstone. From mine own earldom foully ousted me. Tennyson.

A putting out of possession; dispossession; ejection; disseizin. Ouster of the freehold is effected by abatement, intrusion, disseizin, discontinuance, or deforcement. Blackstone. Ouster le main. Etym: [Ouster + F. la main the hand, L. manus.] (Law) A delivery of lands out of the hands of a guardian, or out of the king's hands, or a judgement given for that purpose. Blackstone.

In its original and strict sense, out means from the interior of something; beyond the limits or boundary of somethings; in a position or relation which is exterior to something; -- opposed to in or into. The something may be expressed after of, from, etc. (see Out of, below); or, if not expressed, it is implied; as, he is out; or, he is out of the house, office, business, etc.; he came out; or, he came out from the ship, meeting, sect, party, etc. Out is used in a variety of applications, as: --

Away; abroad; off; from home, or from a certain, or a usual, place; not in; not in a particular, or a usual, place; as, the proprietor is out, his team was taken out. "My shoulder blade is out." Shak. He hath been out (of the country) nine years. Shak.

Beyond the limits of concealment, confinement, privacy, constraint, etc., actual of figurative; hence, not in concealment, constraint, etc., in, or into, a state of freedom, openness, disclosure, publicity, etc.; as, the sun shines out; he laughed out, to be out at the elbows; the secret has leaked out, or is out; the disease broke out on his face; the book is out. Leaves are out and perfect in a month. Bacon. She has not been out [in general society] very long. H. James.

Beyond the limit of existence, continuance, or supply; to the end; completely; hence, in, or into, a condition of extinction, exhaustion, completion; as, the fuel, or the fire, has burned out. "Hear me out." Dryden. Deceitiful men shall not live out half their days. Ps. iv. 23. When the butt is out, we will drink water. Shak.

Beyond possession, control, or occupation; hence, in, or into, a state of want, loss, or deprivation; -- used of office, business, property, knowledge, etc.; as, the Democrats went out and the Whigs came in; he put his money out at interest. "Land that is out at rack rent." Locke. "He was out fifty pounds." Bp. Fell. I have forgot my part, and I am out. Shak.

Beyond the bounds of what is true, reasonable, correct, proper, common, etc.; in error or mistake; in a wrong or incorrect position or opinion; in a state of disagreement, opposition, etc.; in an inharmonious relation. "Lancelot and I are out." Shak. Wicked men are strangely out in the calculating of their own interest. South. Very seldom out, in these his guesses. Addison.
Not in the position to score in playing a game; not in the state or turn of the play for counting or gaining scores.

Improper; unusual; wrong.  -- Out of the woods, not in a place, or state, of obscurity or doubt; free from difficulty or perils; safe. [Colloq.] -- Out to out, from one extreme limit to another, including the whole length, breadth, or thickness; -- applied to measurements.  -- Out West, in or towards, the West; specifically, in some Western State or Territory. [U. S.] -- To come out, To cut out, To fall out, etc. See under Come, Cut, Fall, etc.  -- To put out of the way, to kill; to destroy.  -- Week in, week out. See Day in, day out (above).
One who, or that which, is out; especially, one who is out of office; -- generally in the plural.
A place or space outside of something; a nook or corner; an angle projecting outward; an open space; -- chiefly used in the phrase ins and outs; as, the ins and outs of a question. See under In.
A word or words omitted by the compositor in setting up copy; an omission. To make an out (Print.), to omit something, in setting or correcting type, which was in the copy.
To cause to be out; to eject; to expel. A king outed from his country. Selden. The French have been outed of their holds. Heylin.
To come out with; to make known. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To give out; to dispose of; to sell. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To come or go out; to get out or away; to become public. "Truth will out." Shak.

Expressing impatience, anger, a desire to be rid of; -- with the force of command; go out; begone; away; off. Out, idle words, servants to shallow fools ! Shak. Out upon or on! equivalent to "shame upon!" "away with!" as, out upon you!
To do or beyond; to exceed in acting. [R.] He has made me heir to treasures Would make me outact a real window's whining. Otway.
See lst Fox, 7.
To surpass or conquer in argument.
To utter foolishly or excessively; to surpass in babbling. [R.] Milton.
To outweight; to exceed in weight or effect. Let dull Ajax bear away my right When all his days outbalance this one night. Dryden.
To bar out. [R.] Spenser.
To surpass in begging. [R.]
To exceed or surpass in bidding. Prevent the greedy, and outbid the bold. Pope.
One who outbids. Johnson.
To surpass in bleating.
Inflated with wind. Dryden.
To exceed in blushing; to surpass in rosy color. T. Shipman.
Beyond or outside of the lines of a vessel's bulwarks or hull; in a direction from the hull or from the keel; -- opposed to inboard; as, outboard rigging; swing the davits outboard.
Foreign; not native. [R.]
Outward bound. Dryden.
The farthest or exterior bounds; extreme limits; boundaries. Spenser.
To excel in bowing. Young.
Convex; curved outward. "The convex or outbowed side of a vessel." Bp. Hall.
To surpass in bragging; hence, to make appear inferior. Whose bare outbragg'd the web it seemed to wear. Shak.
To excel in bravery o
To excel in magnificence or comeliness. The basest weed outbraves his dignity. Shak.
To exceed in braying.
To emit with great noise. [Obs.] Fairfax.
To bear down with a brazen face; to surpass in impudence. T. Brown.
A bursting forth; eruption; insurrection. "Mobs and outbreaks." J. H. Newman. The flash and outbreak of a fiery mind. Shak.
The act of breaking out.
That which bursts forth.
To surpass in singing. See Breast, n., 6. [Obs.]
To breathe forth. "Outbreathed life." Spenser.
To cause to be out of breath; to exhaust. Shak.
To issue, as breath; to be breathed out; to exhale. Beau. & Fl.
To surpass in bribing.
To bring or bear out.
To sprout. [Poetic] Spenser.
To exceed in building, or in durability of building.
A building separate from, and subordinate to, the main house; an outhouse.
To exceed in burning.
To burn entirely; to be consumed. Shak.
A bursting forth.
To surpass in canting. Pope.
Cast out; degraded. "Outcast, rejected." Longfellow.

One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home, society, or country; hence, often, a degraded person; a vagabond. The Lord . . . gathereth together the outcasts of Israel. Ps. cxlvii. 2.
A quarrel; a contention. [Scot.] Jamieson.
That which is cast out. [Obs.]
Except. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
To exceed in cheating.
To climb bevond; to surpass in climbing. Davenant.

That which comes out of, or follows from, something else; issue; result; consequence; upshot. "The logical outcome." H. Spenser. All true literature, all genuine poetry, is the direct outcome, the condensed essence, of actual life and thougth. J. C. Shairp.
To exceed the compass or limits of. Bacon.
An outer or exterior court. The skirts and outcourts of heaven. South.
To exceed in cunning. [R.] Shak.
One who cries out or proclaims; a herald or crier.
The coming out of a stratum to the surface of the ground. Lyell.
That part of inclined strata which appears at the surface; basset.
To come out to the surface of the ground; -- said of strata.
A vehement or loud cry; a cry of distress, alarm, opposition, or detestation; clamor.
Sale at public auction. Massinger. Thackeray.
To surpass in daring; to overcome by courage; to brave. Shak. R. Browning.
Being out of date; antiquated. [Obs.] Hammond.
To surpass in dazzing.
To go beyond in performance; to excel; to surpass. An imposture outdoes the original. L' Estrange. I grieve to be outdone by Gay. Swift.
Being, or done, in the open air; being or done outside of certain buildings, as poorhouses, hospitals, etc.; as, outdoor exercise; outdoor relief; outdoor patients.
Abread; out of the house; out of doors.
To draw out; to extract. [R.] "He must the teeth outdraw." Gower.
To pass, or escape, while dreaming. "To oultdream dangers." Beau. & Fl.
To exceed in drinking.
To outlast. [Obs.]
To dwell or stay beyond. [Poetic] "He outdwells his hour." Shak.
One who holds land in a parish, but lives elsewhere. [Eng.]

Being on the outside; external; farthest or farther from the interior, from a given station, or from any space or position regarded as a center or starting place; -- opposed to inner; as, the outer wall; the outer court or gate; the outer stump in cricket; the outer world. Outer bar, in England, the body of junior (or utter) barristers; -- so called because in court they occupy a place beyond the space reserved for Queen's counsel.
The part of a target which is beyond the circles surrounding the bull's-eye.
A shot which strikes the outer of a target.
One who puts out, ousts, or expels; also, an ouster; dispossession. [R.]
Utterly; entirely. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Toward the outside. [R.] Grew.
Being on the extreme external part; farthest outward; as, the outermost row. Boyle.
To face or look (one) out of countenance; to resist or bear down by bold looks or effrontery; to brave. Shak. Having outfaced all the world. South.
The mouth of a river; the lower end of a water course; the open end of a drain, culvert, etc., where the discharge occurs.
A quarrel; a falling out. [Prov. Eng.]
A thief from without or abroad, taken within a lord's fee or liberty.
The privilege of trying such a thief. Burrill.
To exceed in fawning.
To exceed in feasting.
To surpass in feats.
Arable land which has been or is being exhausted. See Infield, 1. [Scot.]
A field beyond, or separated from, the inclosed land about the homestead; an uninclosed or unexplored tract. Also used figuratively. The great outfield of thought or fact. Trench.
The part of the field beyond the diamond, or infield. It is occupied by the fielders.
The part of the field farthest from the batsman.

A fitting out, or equipment, as of a ship for a voyage, or of a person for an expedition in an unoccupied region or residence in a foreign land; things required for equipment; the expense of, or allowance made for, equipment, as by the government of the United States to a diplomatic agent going abroad.
One who furnishes outfits for a voyage, a journey, or a business.
To go beyond, or be superior to, on the flank; to pass around or turn the flank or flanks of.
To exceed in flattering.
A gibe; a contemptuous remark.
A flowing out; efflux.
To flow out. Campbell.
To surpass in flying; to fly beyond or faster than. Shak. Winged with fear outflies the wind. Waller.
To exceed in folly. [R.] Young.
To outrun or outwalk; hence, of a vessel, to outsail. [Colloq.]
External appearance. [Obs.]
To frown down; to overbear by frowning. Shak.
An outlet. [Obs.] Spenser.
To gaze beyond; to exceed in sharpness or persistence of seeing or of looking; hence, to stare out of countenance.
To exceed in generalship; to gain advantage over by superior military skill or executive ability; to outmaneuver. Chesterfield.
To surpass in giving. Dryden.
To go beyond; to exceed in swiftness; to surpass; to outdo.
To circumvent; to overreach. [Obs.] Denham.
That which goes out, or is paid out; outlay; expenditure; -- the opposite of Ant: income. Lowell.
One who goes out or departs.
The act or the state of going out. The outgoings of the morning and evening. Ps. lxv. 8.
That which goes out; outgo; outlay.
The extreme limit; the place of ending. [Obs.] The outgoings of the border were at the north bay of the salt sea, at the south end of Jordan. Josh. xviii. 19.
Going out; departing; as, the outgoing administration; an outgoing steamer.
Ground situated at a distance from the house; outlying land.
To surpass in growing; to grow more than. Shak.
To grow out of or away from; to grow too large, or too aged, for; as, to outgrow clothing; to outgrow usefulness; to outgrow an infirmity.
That which grows out of, or proceeds from, anything; an excrescence; an offshoot; hence, a result or consequence.
A guard or small body of troops at a distance from the main body of an army, to watch for the approach of an enemy; hence, anything for defense placed at a distance from the thing to be defended.
A pouring out; an outburst. A passionate outgush of emotion. Thackeray.
To gush out; to flow forth.
A rope used for hauling out a sail upon a spar; -- opposite of inhaul.
Other. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To surpass (Herod) in violence or wickedness; to exceed in any vicious or offensive particular. "It out-Herods Herod." Shak. Out-Heroding the preposterous fashions of the times. Sir W. Scott.
Outcry; alarm. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To hire out. [Obs.] Spenser.
A small house or building at a little distance from the main house; an outbuilding.
The act of going out; an airing; an excursion; as, a summer outing.
A feast given by an apprentice when he is out of his time. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
To surpass in jesting; to drive out, or away, by jesting. [R.] Shak.
That which jets out or projects from anything. [R.] H. Miller.
To surpass in juggling.
An attachment to a surveyor's compass for keeping tally in chaining.
To surpass in knavery.
To surpass in laboring.
Foreign; outlandish. [Obs.] Strutt.
A foreigner. Wood.
Foreign; not native. Him did outlandish women cause to sin. Neh. xiii. 26. Its barley water and its outlandish wines. G. W. Cable.

Hence: Not according with usage; strange; rude; barbarous; uncouth; clownish; as, an outlandish dress, behavior, or speech. Something outlandish, unearthy, or at variance with ordinary fashion. Hawthorne. --Out*land"ish*ly, adv.  -- Out*land"ish*ness, n.
To exceed in duration; to survive; to endure longer than. Milton.
To surpass or outdo in laughing. Dryden.

To laugh (one) out of a purpose, principle, etc.; to discourage or discomfit by laughing; to laugh down. [R.] His apprehensions of being outlaughed will force him to continue in a restless obscurity. Franklin.
A person excluded from the benefit of the law, or deprived of its protection. Blackstone.
To deprive of the benefit and protection of law; to declare to be an outlaw; to proscribe. Blackstone.
To remove from legal jurisdiction or enforcement; as, to outlaw a debt or claim; to deprive of legal force. "Laws outlawed by necessity." Fuller.
The act of outlawing; the putting a man out of the protection of law, or the process by which a man (as an absconding criminal) is deprived of that protection.
The state of being an outlaw.
To lay out; to spread out; to display. [R.] Drayton.
A laying out or expending.
That which is expended; expenditure.
An outlying haunt. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
To surpass in leaping.
A sally. [R.] Locke.
To excel or surpass in learing.
To learn out [i. e., completely, utterly]; to exhaust knowledge of. Naught, according to his mind, He could outlearn. Spenser. Men and gods have not outlearned it [love]. Emerson.
The place or opening by which anything is let out; a passage out; an exit; a vent. Receiving all, and having no outlet. Fuller.
To let out; to emit. [R.] Daniel.
To exceed in lying. Bp. Hall.
One who does not live where his office, or business, or estate, is. Bentley.
That which lies, or is, away from the main body.
A part of a rock or stratum lying without, or beyond, the main body, from which it has been separated by denudation.
, An extreme member or part of a thing; a limb. [Obs.] Fuller.

synonyms: Sketch; draught; delineation. See Sketch.
definitions: The line which marks the outer limits of an object or figure; the exterior line or edge; contour.
In art: A line drawn by pencil, pen, graver, or the like, by which the boundary of a figure is indicated.
A sketch composed of such lines; the delineation of a figure without shading. Painters, by their outlines, colors, lights, and shadows, represent the same in their pictures. Dryden.

Fig.: A sketch of any scheme; a preliminary or general indication of a plan, system, course of thought, etc.; as, the outline of a speech. But that larger grief . . . Is given in outline and no more. Tennyson.
To draw the outline of.
Fig.: To sketch out or indicate as by an outline; as, to outline an argument or a campaign.
Of or pertaining to an outline; being in, or forming, an outline. Trench.
To live beyond, or longer than; to survive. They live too long who happiness outlive. Dryden.
One who outlives. [R.]
To face down; to outstare. To outlook conquest, and to win renown. Shak.
To inspect throughly; to select. [Obs.] Cotton.
The act of looking out; watch.
One who looks out; also, the place from which one looks out; a watchower. Lyon Playfair.
The view obtained by one looking out; scope of vision; prospect; sight; appearance. Applause Which owes to man's short outlook all its charms. Young.
A loosing from; an escape; an outlet; an evasion. [Obs.] That "whereas" gives me an outloose. Selden.
An excursion. [Obs.] Florio.
To excel in brightness or luster. Shak.
Lying or being at a distance from the central part, or the main body; being on, or beyond, the frontier; exterior; remote; detached.
To surpass, or get an advantage of, in maneuvering; to outgeneral.
To excel in mantling; hence, to excel in splendor, as of dress. [R.] And with poetic trappings grace thy prose, Till it outmantle all the pride of verse. Cowper.
To surpass in marching; to march faster than, or so as to leave behind.
To exceed in measure or extent; to measure more than. Sir T. Browne.
Farthest from the middle or interior; farthest outward; outermost.
To mount above. [R.]
To exceed in naming or describing. [R.]
To exceed in name, fame, or degree. [Obs.] And found out one to outname thy other faults. Beau. & Fl.
The state of being out or beyond; separateness.

The state or quality of being distanguishable from the perceiving mind, by being in space, and possessing marerial quality; externality; objectivity. The outness of the objects of sense. Sir W. Hamiltom.
To exceed in noise; to surpass in noisiness. [R.] Fuller.
To exceed in number.
Being out of the house; being, or done, in the open air; outdoor; as, out-of-door exercise. See Out of door, under Out, adv. Amongst out-of-door delights. G. Eliot.
See under Out, adv.
To outgo; to move faster than; to leave behind. [R.] Lamb.
To exceed in the number of mistresses. [R.] Shak.
A parish lying without the walls of, or in a remote part of, a town. Graunt.
An outlying part. [R.] Ayliffe.
To pass beyond; to exceed in progress.
To exceed in passion.
A patient who is outside a hospital, but receives medical aid from it.
To excel. [R.] Shak.
To grant an outpension to.
A public pension granted to one not required to live in a charitable institution. -- Out"pen`sion*er, n.
To excel or defeat in a game; to play better than; as, to be outplayed in tennis or ball.
To outweigh. Howell.
A harbor or port at some distance from the chief town or seat of trade. Macaulay.
A post or station without the limits of a camp, or at a distance from the main body of an army, for observation of the enemy.
The troops placed at such a station.
To pour out. Milton.
A flowing out; a free discharge.
To excel in power; to overpover. [Obs.] Fuller.
To exceed or excel in prayer.
To surpass in preaching. And for a villain's quick conversion A pillory can outpreach a parson. Trumbull.
To prize beyong value, or in excess; to exceed in value. [Obs.] Shak.
The amount of coal or ore put out from one or more mines, or the quantity of material produced by, or turned out from, one or more furnaces or mills, in a given time.
That which is thrown out as products of the metabolic activity of the body; the egesta other than the fæces. See Income.
The urine, which is assumed to contain all the nitrogen truly excreted by the body, besides a large quantity of saline matters and water. Foster.
To quench entirely; to extinguish. "The candlelight outquenched." Spenser.
To rage in excess of. [R.] Young.

synonyms: Affront; insult; abuse. See Affront.
definitions: Injurious violence or wanton wrong done to persons or things; a gross violation of right or decency; excessive abuse; wanton mischief; gross injury. Chaucer. He wrought great outrages, wasting all the country. Spenser.
Excess; luxury. [Obs.] Chaucer.

To commit outrage upon; to subject to outrage; to treat with violence or excessive abuse. Base and insolent minds outrage men when they have hope of doing it without a return. Atterbury. This interview outrages all decency. Broome.
Specifically, to violate; to commit an indecent assault upon (a female).
To be guilty of an outrage; to act outrageously.

synonyms: Violent; furious; exorbitant; excessive; atrocious; monstrous; wanton; nefarious; heinous. Out*ra"geous*ly, adv. Out*ra"geous*ness, n.
definitions: Of the nature of an outrage; exceeding the limits of right, reason, or decency; involving or doing an outrage; furious; violent; atrocious. "Outrageous weeping." Chaucer. "The most outrageous villainies." Sir P. Sidney. "The vile, outrageous crimes." Shak. "Outrageous panegyric." Dryden.
The utmost or last extremity. Combat à outrance, a fight to the end, or to the death.
To exceed in rank; hence, to take precedence of.
To outshine. [R.] Skelton.
To spread out in array. [Obs.] And now they outray to your fleet. Chapman.
See Outrage, v. i. [Obs.] This warn I you, that ye not suddenly Out of yourself for no woe should outraye. Chaucer.
To obliterate. [Obs.] Sandys.
Being out of the common course or limits; extravagant; bizarre.
To reach beyond.
To excel or surpass in reasoning; to reason better than. South.
To exceed in reckoning or computation. Bp. Pearson.
Excessive presumption. [R.] B. Jonson.
To surpass in giving rede, or counsel. [Obs.] See Atrede. Chaucer.
To go beyond in reigning; to reign through the whole of, or longer than. [R.] Spenser.
To surpass in speed of riding; to ride beyond or faster than. Shak.
A riding out; an excursion. [R.]
A place for riding out. [R.]
A summoner whose office is to cite men before the sheriff. [Obs.]
One who rides out on horseback. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A servant on horseback attending a carriage.
Any spar or projecting timber run out for temporary use, as from a ship's mast, to hold a rope or a sail extended, or from a building, to support hoisting teckle.
A projecting support for a rowlock, extended from the side of a boat.
A boat thus equipped.
A projecting contrivance at the side of a boat to prevent upsetting, as projecting spars with a log at the end.
Immediately; without delay; at once; as, he was killed outright.
Completely; utterly. Cardinal Manning.
To excel in volume of ringing sound; to ring louder than.
To surpass in a rivalry.
To river; to sever. [Obs.] Fairfax.
An excursion. [Obs.] "Outrodes by the ways of Judea." Macc. xv. 41 (Geneva Bible).
To exceed in roaring.
To exceed in romantic character. [R.] Fuller.
An outer room. [R.] Fuller.
To eradicate; to extirpate.

To exceed, or leave behind, in running; to run faster than; to outstrip; to go beyond. Your zeal outruns my wishes. Sir W. Scott. The other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulcher. Jhon xx. 4.
An offshoot; a branch. [R.] "Some outrunner of the river." Lauson.
To rush out; to issue, or ru Garth.
To excel, or to leave behind, in sailing; to sail faster than. Beau. & Fl.
To exceed in odor. Fuller.
To exceed in scolding. Shak.
To confront, or subdue, with greater scorn. Shak.
That which is scoured out o Buckland.
To overpower by disdain; to outface. [Obs.] Marston.
To see beyond; to excel in cer
To exceed in amount of sales; to sell more than.
To exceed in the price of selling; to fetch more than; to exceed in value. Fuller. Shak.
A sentry who guards the entrance or approach to a place; an outguard.
A setting out, starting, or beginning. "The outset of a political journey." Burke. Giving a proper direction to this outset of life. J. Hawes.
One who settles at a distance, or away, from others.
To shine forth. "Bright, outshining beams." Shak.
To excel in splendor. A throne of royal state, which far Outshone the wealth of Ormus and of Ind. Milton.
To exceed or excel in shooting; to shoot beyond. Bacon. Men are resolved never to outshoot their forefathers' mark. Norris.
To shut out. [R.] Donne.

The external part of a thing; the part, end, or side which forms the surface; that which appears, or is manifest; that which is superficial; the exterior. There may be great need of an outside where there is little or nothing within. South. Created beings see nothing but our outside. Addison.
The part or space which lies without an inclosure; the outer side, as of a door, walk, or boundary. I threw open the door of my chamber, and found the family standing on the outside. Spectator.
The furthest limit, as to number, quantity, extent, etc.; the utmost; as, it may last a week at the outside.
One who, or that which, is without; hence, an outside passenger, as distinguished from one who is inside. See Inside, n. 3. [Colloq. Eng.]
Of or pertaining to the outside; external; exterior; superficial.

Reaching the extreme or farthest limit, as to extent, quantity, etc.; as, an outside estimate. [Colloq.] Outside finish (Arch.), a term for the minor parts, as corner boards, hanging stiles, etc., required to complete the exterior of a wooden building; -- rare in masonry.
or prep. On or to the outside (of); without; on the exterior; as, to ride outside the coach; he stayed outside.
One not belonging to the concern, institution, party, etc., spoken of; one disconnected in interest or feeling. [Recent] A. Trollope.
A locksmith's pinchers for grasping the point of a key in the keyhole, to open a door from the outside when the key is inside.
A horse which is not a favorite in the betting. [Cant]
To surpass in singing.
To remain sitting, or in session, longer than, or beyond the time of; to outstay.
A part remote from the center; outer edge; border; -- usually in the plural; as, the outskirts of a town. Wordsworth. The outskirts of his march of mystery. Keble.
To exceed in sleeping. Shak.
To slide outward, onward, or forward; to advance by sliding. [Poetic] At last our grating keels outslide. Whittier.
To soar beyond or above.
The outside sole of a boot or shoe.
To surpass in sounding.
To unyoke or disengage, as oxen from a wagon. [S. Africa]
To exceed in sparkling.
To exceed in speaking.
To speak openly or boldly. T. Campbell.
To express more than. Shak.
To excel in speed. Outspeed the realized miracles of steam. Talfourd.
Outlay; expenditure. [R.] A mere outspend of savageness. I. Taylor.
To spin out; to finish.
Speaking, or spoken, freely, openly, or boldly; as, an outspoken man; an outspoken rebuke.  -- Out*spo"ken*ness, n.
To exceed in sporting. [R.] "Not to outsport discretion." Shak.
To spread out; to expand; -- usually as a past part. or adj.
To spring out; to issue.
To stand out, or project, from a surface or mass; hence, to remain standing out.
To resist effectually; to withstand; to sustain without yielding. [R.] Woodward.
To stay beyond. "I have outstood my time." Shak.
That stands out; undischarged; uncollected; not paid; as, outstanding obligations. Revenues . . . as well outstanding as collected. A. Hamilton.
To excel or overcome in staring; to face down. I would outstare the sternest eyes that look. Shak.
To start out or up. Chaucer.
To stay beyond or longer than. She concluded to outstay him. Mad. D' Arblay.
To exceed in stepping.
To exceed in storming. Insults the tempest and outstorms the skies. J. Barlow.
A street remote from the center of a town. Johnson.
To stretch out. Milton.
To surpass in striding.
To strike out; to strike faster than. Shak.
To go faster than; to outrun; to advance beyond; to leave behing. Appetites which . . . had outstripped the hours. Southey. He still outstript me in the race. Tennyson.
To exceed in suffering.
To exceed in swearing.
To surpass in sweetness. [R.] Shak.
To exceed in swelling.
To swell beyond; to overflow. [Obs.] Hewyt.
Except. [Obs.] R. of Brunne.
or prep. Excepted; save. [Obs.] Wyclif. Chaucer.
To overpower by talking; to exceed in talking; to talk down. Shak.
To surpass in telling, counting, or reckoning. "I have outtold the clock." Beau. & Fl.
An external or superficial thing; outward manner; superficial remark, etc. [Obs.] Not to bear cold forms, nor men's outterms. B. Jonson.
To throw out. Spenser.
To excel in throwing, as in ball playing.
To exceed in toiling.
To silence by talk, clamor, or noise. [R.] Shak.
To overtop. [Obs.]
To exceed in speed o Mad. D' Arblay.
To disentangle. [Obs.]
To exceed in value. Boyle.
To exceed in venom.
To exceed in vying. Dryden.
To exceed in villainy.
To exceed in noise. Shak.
To exceed in the number of votes given; to defeat by votes. South.
To excel in walking; to leave behind in walking. B. Jonson.
The exterior wall; the outside surface, or appearance. Shak.

From the interior part; in a direction from the interior toward the exterior; out; to the outside; beyond; off; away; as, a ship bound outward. The wrong side may be turned outward. Shak. Light falling on them is not reflected outwards. Sir I. Newton. Outward bound, bound in an outward direction or to foreign parts; -- said especially of vessels, and opposed to homeward bound.
Formmg the superficial part; external; exterior; -- opposed to inward; as, an outward garment or layer. Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. Cor. iv. 16.
Of or pertaining to the outer surface or to what is external; manifest; public. "Sins outward." Chaucer. An outward honor for an in ward toil. Shak.
Foreign; not civil or intestine; as, an outward war. [Obs.] Hayward.
Tending to the exterior or outside. The fire will force its outward way. Dryden. -- Out"ward*ly, adv.  -- Out"ward*ness, n. Outward stroke. (Steam Engine) See under Stroke.
External form; exterior. [R.] So fair an outward and such stuff within. Shak.
See Outward, adv.
To exceed in watching.
A way out; exit. [R.] In divers streets and outways multiplied. P. Fletcher.
To wear out; to consume or destroy by wearing. Milton.
To last longer than; to outlast; as, this cloth will outwear the other. "If I the night outwear." Pope.
To weary out. Cowley.
To weed out. [Obs.]
To exceed in weeping.
To exceed in weight or value.
To pour out. [Obs.] Spenser.
To issue forth. Thomson.
imp. of Outgo.
To exceed in lewdness.
To win a way out of. [Obs.]
To extricate by winding; to unloose. [R.] Spenser. Dr. H. More.
To surpass, exceed, or outstrip in flying. Garth.
To surpass in wisdom, esp. in cunning; to defeat or overreach by superior craft. They did so much outwit and outwealth us ! Gauden.
The faculty of acquiring wesdom by observation and experience, or the wisdom so acquired; -- opposed to inwit. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.
To exceed in woe. [Obs.]
To exceed in working; to work more or faster than.
A minor defense constructed beyond the main body of a work, as a ravelin, lunette, hornwork, etc. Wilhelm.
To exceed in worth. [R.]
To extort; to draw from or forth by violence. [Obs.] Spenser.
To exceed or excel in writing.
To exceed in buffoonery. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
Chrome garnet.
See Ooze. [Obs.]
Same as Ousel. The mellow ouzel fluted in the elm. Tennyson.
See Ovum.
Of or pertaining to eggs; done in the egg, or inception; as, oval conceptions. [Obs.]
Having the figure of an egg; oblong and curvilinear, with one end broader than the other, or with both ends of about the same breadth; in popular usage, elliptical.
Broadly elliptical. Oval chuck (Mech.), a lathe chuck so constructed that work attached to it, and cut by the turning tool in the usual manner, becomes of an oval form.

A body or figure in the shape of an egg, or popularly, of an ellipse. Cassinian oval (Geom.), the locus of a point the product of whose distances from two fixed points is constant; -- so called from Cassini, who first investigated the curve. Thus, in the diagram, if P moves so that P A.P B is constant, the point P describes a Cassinian oval. The locus may consist of a single closed line, as shown by the dotted line, or of two equal ovals about the points A and B.
The albumin from white of eggs; egg albumin; -- in distinction from serum albumin. See Albumin.
Having the form of an egg; having a figure such that any section in the direction of the shorter diameter will be circular, and any in the direction of the longer diameter will be oval.
In an oval form.
Exultant. [Obs.] Holland.
Of or pertaining to an ovary.
One of the tubes of which the ovaries of most insects are composed.
One who performs, or is skilled in, ovariotomy.
The operation of removing one or both of the ovaries; oöphorectomy.
Consisting of eggs; as, ovarious food. [R.] Thomson.
Inflammation of the ovaries.
An ovary. See Ovary.
That part of the pistil which contains the seed, and in most flowering plants develops into the fruit. See Illust. of Flower.
The essential female reproductive organ in which the ova are produced. See Illust. of Discophora.
Shaped like an egg, with the lower extremity broadest.
Having the shape of an egg, or of the longitudinal sectior of an egg, with the broader end basal. Gray.
Having an ovate form, but narrowed at the end into a slender point.
Having a form intermediate between ovate and cylindraceous.
Ovate.
Having a form intermediate between ovate and lanceolate.
Oblong. with one end narrower than the other; ovato-oblong.
Having a form intermediate between that of an egg and a sphere; roundly ovate.
Having an ovate form, but with a subulate tip or extremity.
A lesser kind of triumph allowed to a commander for an easy, bloodless victory, or a victory over slaves.
Hence: An expression of popular homage; the tribute of the multitude to a public favorite. To rain an April of ovation round Their statues. Tennyson.
Same as Ovate-acuminate.
Same as Ovate-cylindraceous.
Same as Ovate-oblong.
Same as Ovate-rotundate.

A place arched over with brick or stonework, and used for baking, heating, or drying; hence, any structure, whether fixed or portable, which may be heated for baking, drying, etc.; esp., now, a chamber in a stove, used for baking or roasting.
Any species of the genus Furnarius, allied to the creepers. They inhabit South America and the West Indies, and construct curious oven-shaped nests.
In the United States, Seiurus aurocapillus; -- called also golden-crowned thrush.
In England, sometimes applied to the willow warbler, and to the long-tailed titmouse.

Above, or higher than, in place or position, with the idea of covering; -- opposed to Ant: under; as, clouds are over our heads; the smoke rises over the city. The mercy seat that is over the testimony. Ex. xxx. 6. Over them gleamed far off the crimson banners of morning. Longfellow.

Across; from side to side of; -- implying a passing or moving, either above the substance or thing, or on the surface of it; as, a dog leaps over a stream or a table. Certain lakes . . . poison birds which fly over them. Bacon.
Upon the surface of, or the whole surface of; hither and thither upon; throughout the whole extent of; as, to wander over the earth; to walk over a field, or over a city.
Above; -- implying superiority in excellence, dignity, condition, or value; as, the advantages which the Christian world has over the heathen. Swift.

Above in authority or station; -- implying government, direction, care, attention, guard, responsibility, etc.; -- opposed to Ant: under. Thou shalt be over my house. Gen. xli. 40. I will make thee rules over many things. Matt. xxv. 23. Dost thou not watch over my sin Job xiv. 16. His tender mercies are over all his works. Ps. cxlv. 9.
Across or during the time of; from beginning to end of; as, to keep anything over night; to keep corn over winter.
Above the perpendicular height or length of, with an idea of measurement; as, the water, or the depth of water, was over his head, over his shoes.
Beyond; in excess of; in addition to; more than; as, it cost over five dollars. "Over all this." Chaucer.
Above, implying superiority after a contest; in spite of; notwithstanding; as, he triumphed over difficulties; the bill was passed over the veto.
From one side to another; from side to side; across; crosswise; as, a board, or a tree, a foot over, i. e., a foot in diameter.

From one person or place to another regarded as on the opposite side of a space or barrier; -- used with verbs of motion; as, to sail over to England; to hand over the money; to go over to the enemy. "We will pass over to Gibeah." Judges xix. 12. Also, with verbs of being: At, or on, the opposite side; as, the boat is over.
From beginning to end; throughout the course, extent, or expanse of anything; as, to look over accounts, or a stock of goods; a dress covered over with jewels.
From inside to outside, above or across the brim. Good measure, pressed down . . . and running over. Luke vi. 38.
Beyond a limit; hence, in excessive degree or quantity; superfluously; with repetition; as, to do the whole work over. "So over violent." Dryden. He that gathered much had nothing over. Ex. xvi. 18.
In a manner to bring the under side to or towards the top; as, to turn (one's self) over; to roll a stone over; to turn over the leaves; to tip over a cart.
At an end; beyond the limit of continuance; completed; finished. "Their distress was over." Macaulay. "The feast was over." Sir W. Scott.
Upper; covering; higher; superior; also, excessive; too much or too great; -- chiefly used in composition; as, overshoes, overcoat, over-garment, overlord, overwork, overhaste.
A certain number of balls (usually four) delivered successively from behind ine wicket, after which the ball is bowled from behing the other wicket as many times, the fielders changing places.
To be exceedingly plenty or superabundant. Pope.
To act or perform to excess; to exaggerate in acting; as, he overacted his part.
To act upon, or influence, unduly. [Obs.] The hope of inheritance overacts them. Milton.
To act more than is necessary; to go to excess in action. B. Jonson.
Per
To affect or care for unduly. [Obs.] Milton.
To agitate or discuss beyond what is expedient. Bp. Hall.
Everywhere. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A kind of loose trousers worn over others to protect them from soiling.
Waterproof leggings. R. D. Blackmore.
The state of being overanxious; excessive anxiety.
Anxious in an excessive or needless degree.  -- O"ver*anx"ious*ly, adv.
To make or place an arch over; to hang over like an arch. "Brown with o'erarching shades." Pope.
Done (as bowling or pitching) with the arm raised above the shoulder. See Overhard. "An over-arm with a round-arm bowler." R. A. Proctor.
To awe exceedingly; to subjugate or restrain by awe or great fear. The king was present in person to overlook the magistrates, and overawe these subjects with the terror of his sword. Spenser.
Awful, or reverential, in an excessive degree. [R.] Milton.
To exceed equality with; to outweigh. Locke.
To cause to lose balance or equilibrium.
Excess of weight or value; something more than an equivalent; as, an overbalance of exports. J. Edwards.
Excessively barren.
Excessively fertile; bearing rank or noxious growths. [Obs.] "Overbattle grounds." Hooker.

To bear down or carry down, as by excess of weight, power, force, etc.; to overcome; to suppress. The point of reputation, when the news first came of the battle lost, did overbear the reason of war. Bacon. Overborne with weight the Cyprians fell. Dryden. They are not so ready to overbear the adversary who goes out of his own country to meet them. Jowett (Thucyd. )
To domineer over; to overcome by insolence.
To bear fruit or offspring to excess; to be too prolific.
Overpowering; subduing; repressing. I. Watts.
Aggressively haughty; arrogant; domineering; tyrannical; dictatorial; insolent. --O`ver*bear"ing*ly, adv.  -- O`ver*bear"ing*ness, n.
To bend to excess.
To bend over. [R.]
To bid or offer beyond, or in excess of. Dryden.
To outlive. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To blow over, or be subdued. [R.] Spenser.
To force so much wind into a pipe that it produces an overtone, or a note higher than the natural note; thus, the upper octaves of a flute are produced by overblowing.
To blow away; to dissipate by wind, or as by wind. When this cloud of sorrow's overblown. Waller.
Over the side of a ship; hence, from on board of a ship, into the water; as, to fall overboard. To throw overboard, to discard; to abandon, as a dependent or friend.
To boil over or unduly. Nor is discontent to keep the mind Deep in its fountain, lest it overboil In the hot throng. Byron.
Excessively or presumptuously bold; impudent. Shak.  -- O"ver*bold"ly, adv.
Excessively bookish.
Bounteous to excess.
To bend or bow over; to bend in a contrary direction. [Obs.] Fuller.
To breed to excess.
To flow over the brim; to be so full as to overflow. [R.]
To hang over like a brow; to impend over. [Poetic] Longfellow. Did with a huge projection overbrow Large space beneath. Wordsworth.
To build over. Milton.
To build too much; to build beyond the demand.
Having too many buildings; as, an overbuilt part of a town.
To oppress by bulk; to overtower. [Obs. & R.] Shak.
To load with too great weight or too much care, etc. Sir P. Sidney.
The waste which overlies good stone in a quarry. Raymond.
Too burdensome.
To burn too much; to be overzealous.
Too busy; officious.
To buy too much.
To buy at too dear a rate. Dryden.
To cover as with a canopy. Shak.
Too capable. [R.] Overcapable of such pleasing errors. Hooker.
Excessive care. Dryden.
Too careful. Shak.
Too anxious; too full of care. [Archaic] Fuller.
To carry too far; to carry beyond the proper point. Hayward.
To cast or cover over; hence, to cloud; to darken. Those clouds that overcast your morn shall fly. Dryden.
To compute or rate too high. Bacon.
To take long, loose stitches over (the raw edges of a seam) to prevent raveling.
To overtake. [Obs.]
Too cautious; cautious or prudent to excess.  -- O"ver*cau"tious*ly, adv.  -- O"ver*cau"tiou*ness, n.
Too much or too frequent change; fickleness. [R.] Beau. & Fl.
To charge or load too heavily; to burden; to oppress; to cloy. Sir W. Raleigh.
To fill too full; to crowd. Our language is overcharged with consonants. Addison.
To charge excessively; to charge beyond a fair rate or price.
To exaggerate; as, to overcharge a description. Overcharged mine. (Mil.) See Globe of compression, under Globe.
To make excessive charges.
An excessive load or burden.
An excessive charge in an account.
To climb over. Surrey.
To cover or overspread with clouds; to becloud; to overcast.
To fill beyond satiety. Shak.
A coat worn over the other clothing; a greatcoat; a topcoat.
Cold to excess. Wiseman.
To color too highly.

synonyms: conquer; subdue; vanquish; overpower; overthrow; overturn; defeat; crush; overbear; overwhelm; prostrate; beat; surmount. See Conquer.
definitions: To get the better of; to surmount; to conquer; to subdue; as, to overcome enemies in battle. This wretched woman overcome Of anguish, rather than of crime, hath been. Spenser.
To overflow; to surcharge. [Obs.] J. Philips.
To come or pass over; to spreads over. [Obs.] And overcome us like a summer's cloud. Shak.
To gain the superiority; to be victorious. Rev. iii. 21.
One who overcomes.
Conquering; subduing.  -- O`ver*com"ing*ly, adv.
Excessive confidence; too great reliance or trust.
Confident to excess.  -- O"ver*con"fi*dent*ly, adv.
Too costly. Milton.
To rate too high; to outnumber. Shak.
To cover up. Shak.
Too credulous.
To crow, exult, or boast, over; to overpower. Spenser. Shak.
To crowd too much.
Exceedingly or excessively cunning.
Too curious.
To dare too much or rashly; to be too daring.
To date later than the true or proper period. Milton.
The excess. [Obs.] The overdeal in the price will be double. Holland.
Too delicate.
Delighted beyond measure.
To develop excessively; specif. (Photog.),
to subject (a plate or film) too long to the developing process.
Covered over. [Obs.] Spenser.
To do too much; to exceed what is proper or true in doing; to exaggerate; to carry too far. Anything so overdone is from the purpose of playing. Shak.
To overtask. or overtax; to fatigue; to exhaust; as, to overdo one's strength.
To surpass; to excel. [R.] Tennyson.
To cook too much; as, to overdo the meat.
To labor too hard; to do too much.
One who overdoes.
To dose to excess; to give an overdose, or too many doses, to.
Too great a dose; an excessive dose.
The act of overdrawing; also, the amount or sum overdrawn.
To exaggerate; to overdo.
To make drafts upon or against, in excess of the proper amount or limit.
To dress or adorn to excess; to dress too much. Pope.
To drink to excess.
To drive too hard, or far, or beyond strength.
To wet or drench to excess. [Obs.] W. Browne.
To dry too much. Burton.
Due and more than due; delayed beyond the proper time of arrival or payment, etc.; as, an overdue vessel; an overdue note.
To dye with excess of color; to put one color over (another). Shak.
Too eager; too impatient.  -- O`ver*ea"ger*ly, adv.  -- O"ver*ea"ger*ness, n.
Too earnest.  -- O"ver*ear"nest*ly, adv.  -- O"ver*ear"nest*ness, n.
To gnaw all over, or on all sides. [Obs.] Shak.
To eat to excess; -- often with a reflexive.
Too elegant. Johnson.
To make too empty; to exhaust. [R.] Carew.
Uppermost; outermost. Full threadbare was his overeste courtepy. Chaucer.
To estimate too highly; to overvalue.
An estimate that is too high; as, an overestimate of the vote.
To excite too much.
Excess of excitement; the state of being overexcited.
To exert too much.
Excessive exertion.
To expose excessively; specif. (Photog.),
to subject (a plate or film) too long to the actinic action of the light used in producing a picture. -- O`ver*ex*po"sure (#), n.
Too exquisite; too exact or nice; too careful.
To superintend; to oversee; to inspect. [Obs.]
To see; to observe. [Obs.] Shak.
A cataract; a waterfall. [Obs.]
A turbulent surface of water, caused by strong currents setting over submerged ridges; also, a dangerous submerged ridge or shoal.
Excessive fatigue.
To fatigue to excess; to tire out.
To feed to excess; to surfeit.
Excessively fierce.
To fill to excess; to surcharge.
To fish to excess.
To overflow. [R.] Dryden.
To make excessive display or flourish of. Collier.
To embellish with outward ornaments or flourishes; to varnish over. [Obs.] Shak.
To flow over; to cover woth, or as with, water or other fluid; to spread over; to inundate; to overwhelm. The northern nations overflowed all Christendom. Spenser.
To flow over the brim of; to fill more than full.
To run over the bounds.
To be superabundant; to abound. Rogers.
A flowing over, as of water or other fluid; an inundation. Bacon.
That which flows over; a superfluous portion; a superabundance. Shak.
An outlet for the escape of surplus liquid. Overflow meeting, a meeting constituted of the surplus or overflow of another audience.
An overflow; that which overflows; exuberance; copiousness. He was ready to bestow the overflowings of his full mind on anybody who would start a subject. Macaulay.
In great abundance; exuberantly. Boyle.
To flush to excess. [R.]
To flutter over.
Overflow; exuberance. [R.]
To cross or pass over by flight. Byron.
, Milton.  -- O"ver*fond"ly, adv.  -- O"ver*fond"ness, n.
Excessive force; violence.
Forward to excess; too forward.  -- O"ver*for"ward*ness, n.
Free to excess; too liberal; too familiar.  -- O"ver*free"ly, adv.
To put too much freight in or upon; to load too full, or too heavily; to overload.
Too frequent.
To cover with a frieze, or as with a frieze. E. Hall.
To confront; to oppose; to withstand. [Obs.] Milton.
Too fruitful.
Too full; filled to overflowing; excessively full; surfeited. Shak.
The state of being excessively or abnormally full, so as to cause overflow, distention, or congestion; excess of fullness; surfeit.
An outer garment.
To garrison to excess.
To gaze; to overlook. [Poetic] "Earth's o'ergazing mountains." Byron.
To reach; to overtake; to pass. [Obs.]
To get beyond; to get over or recover from. [R.]
To gild over; to varnish.
To gird too closely. [R.]
To give over; to surrender; to yield. [Obs.] Spenser.
Excessively or unduly glad.
To glance over.

Applied over the glaze; -- said of enamel paintings, which sometimes are seen to project from the surface of the ware. (b) Suitable for applying upon the glaze; -- said of vitrifiable colors used in ceramic decoration.
To glide over. Wyatt.
To spread gloom over; to make gloomy; to overshadow. [R.] Overgloomed by memories of sorrow. De Quincey.
To travel over. [R.] Shak.
To exceed; to surpass. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
To cover. [Obs.] Chapman.
To oppress; to weigh down. [Obs.] Shak.
To gorge to excess.
To grace or honor exceedingly or beyond desert. [R.] Beau. & Fl.
Overstocked, or overgrown, or covered, with grass. [Obs.] Spenser.
Too great.
Excessive greatness.
Excessively greedy.
Too gross.
Situated over or above ground; as, the overground portion of a plant.
To grow over; to cover with growth or herbage, esp. that which is rank. The green . . . is rough and overgrown. Sir W. Scott.
To grow beyond; to rise above; hence, to overcome; to oppress. [Obs.] Mortimer. "O'ergrown with labor." Beau. & Fl. [Usually in the past participle.]
To grow beyond the fit or natural size; as, a huge, overgrown ox. L'Estrange.
Excessive growth.
See Overhaul. [Obs.]
See Overhaul. [Obs.]
The upper hand; advantage; superiority; mastery. He had gotten thereby a great overhand on me. Sir T. More.
Over and over; -- applied to a style of sewing, or to a seam, in which two edges, usually selvedges, are sewed together by passing each stitch over both.
Done (as pitching or bowling) with the hand higher than the elbow, or the arm above, or higher than, the shoulder. Overhand knot. See Illustration of Knot.
In an overhand manner or style.
To handle, or use, too much; to mention too often. Shak.
To impend or hang over. [R.] Beau. & Fl.
To hang over; to jut or project over. Pope.
To jut over. Milton.
In a general sense, that which just out or projects; a projection; also, the measure of the projection; as, the overhang is five feet.
Specifically: The projection of an upper part (as a roof, an upper story, or other part) of a building beyond the lower part; as, the overhang of a roof, of the eaves, etc.
The portion of the bow or stem of a vessel that projects over the water beyond the water line.
The projection of a part beyond another part that is directly below it, or beyond a part by which it is supported; as, the overhang of a shaft; i. e., its projection beyond its bearing.
Exceedingly happy. Shak.
To harden too much; to make too hard. Boyle.
Too hardy; overbold.
Too great haste.
Too hasty; precipitate; rash.  -- O"ver*has"ti*ly, adv.  -- O`ver*has"ti*ness, n.
To haul or drag over; hence, to turn over for examination; to inspect; to examine thoroughly with a view to corrections or repairs.
To gain upon in a chase; to overtake. To overhaul a tackle, to pull on the leading parts so as to separate the blocks.  -- To overhaul running rigging, to keep it clear, and see that no hitch occurs.
A strict examination with a view to correction or repairs.
Aloft; above; in or attached to the ceiling or roof; in the story or upon the floor above; in the zenith. While overhead the moon Sits arbitress. Milton.

Those general charges or expenses in any business which cannot be charged up as belonging exclusively to any particular part of the work or product, as where different kinds of goods are made, or where there are different departments in a business; -- called also fixed, establishment, or (in a manufacturing business) administration, selling, and distribution, charges, etc.
To hear more of (anything) than was intended to be heard; to hear by accident or artifice. Shak.
To hear again. ShaK.
To heat to excess; to superheat. Cowper.
Excessively heavy.
To hele or cover over. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
To overtake. [Obs.] So forth he went and soon them overhent. Spenser.
Too high.
Too highly; too greatly.
To pass over by, or as by a hop; to skip over; hence, to overpass. [Obs.] "When the time is overhipt." Holland.
To hold or value too highly; to estimate at too dear a rate. [Obs.] Shak.
Covered over; ornamented with hangings. Carlyle.
Suspended from above or from the top. Overhung door, a sliding door, suspended door, suspended from the top, as upon rollers.
To influence in an excessive degree; to have undue influence over.
To inform, fill, or animate, excessively. [R.] Johnson.
An excessive issue; an issue, as of notes or bonds, exceeding the limit of capital, credit, or authority. An overissue of government paper. Brougham.
To issue in excess.
Excessively jealous; too jealous.
To make excessively joyful; to gratify extremely.
Excessive joy; transport.
To jump over; hence, to omit; to ignore. Marston.
A king who has sovereignty over inferior kings or ruling princes. J. R. Green.
Too knowing or too cunning.
To cause to labor excessively; to overwork. Dryden.
To labor upon excessively; to refine unduly.
To load with too great a cargo; to overburden; to overload. Spenser.
Being, or accomplished, over the land, instead of by sea; as, an overland journey.
By, upon, or across, land.
One who travels over lands or countries; one who travels overland.
Employing too many words; diffuse. Lowell.
To lap over; to lap.
The lapping of one thing over another; as, an overlap of six inches; an overlap of a slate on a roof.
An extension of geological beds above and beyond others, as in a conformable series of beds, when the upper beds extend over a wider space than the lower, either in one or in all directions.
Too large; too great.
Excess of size or bulk.
To drive on rashly; to go to excess; hence, to exaggerate; to boast. [Obs.] Barrow.
Excess; exaggeration. [Obs.]
Too late; exceedingly late.
To lave or bathe over.
Lavish to excess.

To lay, or spread, something over or across; hence, to cover; to overwhelm; to press excessively upon. When any country is overlaid by the multitude which live upon it. Sir W. Raleigh. As when a cloud his beams doth overlay. Spenser. Framed of cedar overlaid with gold. Milton. And overlay With this portentous bridge the dark abyss. Milton.
To smother with a close covering, or by lying upon. This woman's child died in the night; because she overlaid it. 1 Kings iii. 19. A heap of ashes that o'erlays your fire. Dryden.
To put an overlay on.
A covering. Sir W. Scott.
A piece of paper pasted upon the tympan sheet to improve the impression by making it stronger at a particular place.
One who overlays; that with which anything is overlaid.
A superficial covering; a coating.
To domineer over; to affront; to treat with indignity. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To leap over or across; hence, to omit; to ignore. "Let me o'erleap that custom." Shak.
Too learned.  -- O"ver*learn"ed, adv.  -- O"ver*learn"ed*ness, n.
Upper leather. Shak.
To leaven too much; hence, to change excessively; to spoil. [Obs.]
Too liberal.
In an overliberal manner.
To lick over.
To lie over or upon; specifically, to suffocate by lying upon; as, to overlie an infant. Quain. A woman by negligence overlieth her child in her sleeping. Chaucer.
Too strong a light. Bacon.
Too light or frivolous; giddy.
The quality or state of being overly; carelessness. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
To cause to linger; to detain too long. [Obs.] Fuller.
The upper lip. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To outlive. Sir P. Sidney. The culture of Northumbria overlived the term of its political supermacy. Earle.
To live too long, too luxuriously, or too actively. Milton. "Overlived in this close London life." Mrs. Browning.
A survivor. Bacon.
To load or fill to excess; to load too heavily.
An excessive load; the excess beyond a proper load.
Excessively logical; adhering too closely to the forms or rules of logic.
Too long. Shak.

To look down upon from a place that is over or above; to look over or view from a higher position; to rise above, so as to command a view of; as, to overlook a valley from a hill. "The pile o'erlooked the town." Dryden. [Titan] with burning eye did hotly overlook them. Shak.
Hence: To supervise; to watch over; sometimes, to observe secretly; as, to overlook a gang of laborers; to overlook one who is writing a letter.
To inspect; to examine; to look over carefully or repeatedly. "Overlook this pedigree." Shak. The time and care that are required To overlook and file and polish well. Roscommon.
To look upon with an evil eye; to bewitch by looking upon; to fascinate. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Shak. If you trouble me I will overlook you, and then your pigs will die. C. Kingsley.

To look over and beyond (anything) without seeing it; to miss or omit in looking; hence, to refrain from bestowing notice or attention upon; to neglect; to pass over without censure or punishment; to excuse. The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. Acts xvii. 30 (Rev. Ver. ) They overlook truth in the judgments they pass. Atterbury. The pardoning and overlooking of faults. Addison.
One who overlooks.
See Orlop. [Obs.]
One who is lord over another or others; a superior lord; a master. Freeman.
Lordship or supremacy of a person or a people over others. J. R. Green.
Too loud; noisy.
To love to excess.
Excessively luscious.
Too lusty, or lively. Shak.
Careless; negligent; inattentive; superfical; not thorough. [Archaic] Bp. Hall.
Excessive; too much. [R.] Coleridge.
In an overly manner. [Archaic]
Lying over or upon something; as, overlying rocks.
To magnify too much. Bp. Hall.
Excessively malapert or impudent. [Obs.] Prynne.
One in authority over others; a chief; usually, an overseer or boss.
An arbiter.
In the philosophy of Nietzsche, a man of superior physique and powers capable of dominating others; one fitted to survive in an egoistic struggle for the mastery.
In an excessive manner; excessively. [Obs.] Wiclif.
To march too far, or too much; to exhaust by marching. Baker.
To furnish (a vessel) with too long or too heavy a mast or masts.
To overpower; to subdue; to vanquish; to govern.
To be more than equal to or a match for; hence, to vanquish. Drayton.
To marry (one) to a superior. [Obs.] Burton.
One superior in power; also, an unequal match; a contest in which one of the opponents is overmatched. Milton. D. Webster.
To measure or estimate too largely.
Excessive measure; the excess beyond true or proper measure; surplus.
To meddle unduly.
Excessive interference. "Justly shent for their overmeddling." Fuller.
Too mellow; overripe.
Excessive merit. Bacon.
Overmuch. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
To mix with too much.
Modest to excess; bashful.  -- O"ver*mod"est*ly, adv.
Excessively moist. Bacon.
Excess of moisture.
Beyond; moreover. [Obs.]
The day after or following to-morrow. [Obs.] Bible (1551).
Over the rest in authority; above all others; highest. [Obs.] Fabyan.
To mount over; to go higher than; to rise above.
Too much.  -- adv.
In too great a degree; too much.  -- n.
An excess; a surplus.
The quality or state of being in excess; superabundance. [R.] B. Jonson.
To multiply or increase too much; to repeat too often.
To outnumber. [Obs.]
To name over or in a series; to recount. [Obs.] Shak.
Excessively neat. Spectator.
Excessively nice; fastidious. Bp. Hall.  -- O"ver*nice"ly, adv.  -- O"ver*nice"ness, n.
The fore part of the night last past; the previous evening. [R.] Shak.
In the fore part of the night last past; in the evening before; also, during the night; as, the candle will not last overnight. I had been telling her all that happened overnight. Dickens.
To overpower by noise.
Excessively numerous; too many.
To domineer over by virtue of office. [Obs.] Shak.
Too busy; too ready to intermeddle; too officious. Collier.
To color or describe too strongly. Sir W. Raleigh.
To pamper excessively; to feed or dress too much. Dryton.
To give too important or difficult a part to. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
To go over or beyond; to cross; as, to overpass a river; to overpass limits.
To pass over; to omit; to overlook; to disregard. All the beauties of the East He slightly viewed and slightly overpassed. Milton.
To surpass; to excel. [R.] R. Browning.
To pass over, away, or off.
Passionate to excess.  -- O"ver*pas"sion*ate*ly, adv.
Patient to excess.
To pay too much to; to reward too highly.
To peer over; to rise above.
To people too densely.
To perch upon; to fly over. [Obs.] Shak.
To persuade or influence against one's inclination or judgment. Pope.
To pester exceedingly or excessively. Sir W. Raleigh.
To surpass nature in the picture or representation of. [Obs.] "O'erpicturing that Venus." Shak.
To please excessively.
That which remains after a supply, or beyond a quantity proposed; surplus. Shak. "The overplus of a great fortune." Addison.
To ply to excess; to exert with too much vigor; to overwork. Milton.
To outweigh; to overbalance. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
Preponderant weight; a counterbalance. [R.] Mrs. Browning.
To polish too much.
Too heavy.
To post over; to pass over swiftly, as by post. Shak.
Too potent or powerful.

synonyms: overbear; overcome; vanquish; defeat; crush; overwhelm; overthrow; rout; conquer; subdue.
definitions: To excel or exceed in power; to cause to yield; to vanquish; to subdue; as, the light overpowers the eyes. "And overpower'd that gallant few." Wordsworth.
A dominating power. Bacon.
Excelling in power; too powerful; irresistible.  -- O`ver*pow"er*ing*ly, adv.
To praise excessively or unduly.
The act of praising unduly; excessive praise. Milton.
To bear upon with irresistible force; to crush; to overwhelm. Shak.
To overcome by importunity. Johnson.
Excessive pressure or urging. London Athenæum.
Toprize excessively; to overvalue. Sir H. Wotton.
Excessive production; supply beyond the demand. J. S. Mill.
Too prompt; too ready or eager; precipitate.  -- O`ver*prompt"ness, n.
Containing more alcohol than proof spirit; stronger than proof spirit; that is, containing more than 49.3 per cent by weight of alcohol.
To make of too great proportion.
Exceedingly or unduly proud. "Overproud of his victory." Milton.
Too provident.
To provoke excessively. Bp. Hall.
To quell or subdue completely. [R.] Bp. Hall.
Too much quietness. Sir. T. Browne.
To rake over, or sweep across, from end to end, as waves that break over a vessel anchored with head to the sea.
Too rank or luxuriant.
To rate or value too highly.
An excessive rate. [R.] Massinger.
To reach above or beyond in any direction.
To deceive, or get the better of, by artifice or cunning; to outwit; to cheat. Shak.
To reach too far; as:
To strike the toe of the hind foot against the heel or shoe of the forefoot; -- said of horses.
To cheat by cunning or deception.
The act of striking the heel of the fore foot with the toe of the hind foot; -- said of horses.
One who overreaches; one who cheats; a cheat.
To read over, or peruse. Shak.
Too ready.  -- O"ver*read"*i*ly, adv.  -- O"ver*read"i*ness, n.
To reckon too highly.
To smear with red. [Obs.]
To refine too much.
Excessive refinement.
To rent for too much.
Exccessively rich.
To ride over or across; to ride upon; to trample down. The carter overridden with [i. e., by] his cart. Chaucer.
To suppress; to destroy; to supersede; to annul; as, one low overrides another; to override a veto.
To ride beyond; to pass; to outride. [Obs.] I overrode him on the way. Shak.
To ride too much; to ride, as a horse, beyond its strength.
Having too much rigging.
Excessively righteous; -- usually implying hypocrisy.
Too rigid; too severe.
Too rigorous; harsh.
Matured to excess. Milton.
To make too ripe. Shak.
To roast too much. Shak.
To rule over; to govern or determine by superior authority.

To rule or determine in a contrary way; to decide against; to abrogate or alter; as, God overrules the purposes of men; the chairman overruled the point of order. His passion and animosity overruled his conscience. Clarendon. These [difficulties] I had habitually overruled. F. W. Newman.
To supersede, reject, annul, or rule against; as, the plea, or the decision, was overruled by the court.
To be superior or supreme in rulling or controlling; as, God rules and overrules. Shak.
One who, or that which, controls, governs, or determines. Sir P. Sidney.
Exerting controlling power; as, an overruling Providence.  -- O`ver*rul"ing*ly, adv.

To run over; to grow or spread over in excess; to invade and occupy; to take possession of; as, the vine overran its trellis; the farm is overrun with witch grass. Those barbarous nations that overran the world. Spenser.
To exceed in distance or speed of running; to go beyond or pass in running. Ahimaaz run by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi. 2 Sam. xviii. 23.
To go beyond; to extend in part beyond; as, one line overruns another in length.
To abuse or oppress, as if by treading upon. None of them the feeble overran. Spenser.
To carry over, or back, as type, from one line or page into the next after, or next before.
To extend the contents of (a line, column, or page) into the next line, column, or page.
To run, pass, spread, or flow over or by something; to be beyond, or in excess. Despised and trodden down of all that overran. Spenser.
To extend beyond its due or desired length; as, a line, or advertisement, overruns.
One that overruns. Lovelace.
To saturate to excess.
To say over; to repeat. Ford.
Scented excessively.
Covered or concealed by a different odor. Fuller.
Overscrupulousness.
Scrupulous to excess.
The quality or state of being overscrupulous; excess of scrupulousness.
Beyond the sea; foreign.
Over the sea; abroad. Milton. Tennyson.
To search all over.
To season too highly.
To superintend; to watch over; to direct; to look or see after; to overlook.
To omit or neglect seeing. Spenser.

To see too or too much; hence, to be deceived. [Obs.] The most expert gamesters may sometimes oversee. Fuller. Your partiality to me is much overseen, if you think me fit to correct your Latin. Walpole.
One who oversees; a superintendent; a supervisor; as, an overseer of a mill; specifically, one or certain public officers; as, an overseer of the poor; an overseer of highways.
The office of an overseer.
To sell for a higher price than; to exceed in selling price. One whose beauty Would oversell all Italy. Beau. & Fl.

To sell beyond means of delivery. [Brokers'Cant] Oversold market (Brokers' Cant), a market in which stocks or commodities have been sold "short" to such an extent that it is difficult to obtain them for delivery.
To turn or tip (anything) over from an upright, or a proper, position so that it lies upon its side or bottom upwards; to upset; as, to overset a chair, a coach, a ship, or a building. Dryden.
To cause to fall, or to tail; to subvert; to overthrow; as, to overset a government or a plot. Addison.
To fill too full. [Obs.] Howell.
To turn, or to be turned, over; to be upset. Mortimer.
An upsetting; overturn; overthrow; as, the overset of a carriage.
An excess; superfluity. [Obs.] "This overset of wealth and pomp. " Bp. Burnel.
To cover with shade; to render dark or gloomy; to overshadow. Shak.
To throw a shadow, or shade, over; to darken; to obscure. There was a cloud that overshadowed them. Mark ix. 7.
Fig.: To cover with a superior influence. Milton.
One that throws a shade, or shadow, over anything. Bacon.
Overshadowing. [R.]
To shake over or away; to drive away; to disperse. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To shine over or upon; to illumine. Shak.
To excel in shining; to outshine. Shak.
A shoe that is worn over another for protection from wet or for extra warmth; esp., an India-rubber shoe; a galoche.
To shoot over or beyond. "Not to overshoot his game." South.
To pass swiftly over; to fly beyond. Hartle.
To exceed; as, to overshoot the truth. Cowper. To overshoot one's self, to venture too far; to assert too much.
To fly beyond the mark. Collier.

From Overshoot, v. t. Overshot wheel, a vertical water wheel, the circumference of which is covered with cavities or buckets, and which is turned by water which shoots over the top of it, filling the buckets on the farther side and acting chiefly by its we'ght.

synonyms: Superintendence; supervision; inspection; overlooking; inadvertence; neglect; mistake; error; omission.
definitions: Watchful care; superintendence; general supervision.
An overlooking; an omission; an error. Hooker.
Escape from an overlooked peril. [R.] "His fool-happy oversight." Spenser.
To surpass in size.
To cover with viscid matter. [R.] O'ersized with coagulate gore. Shak.
To skip or leap over; to treat with indifference. Shak.
An upper skirt, shorter than the dress, and usually draped.
A bar in a river; as, the overslaugh in the Hudson River. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.

To hinder or stop, as by an overslaugh or an impediment; as, to overslaugh a bill in a legislative body; to overslaugh a military officer, that is, to hinder his promotion or employment. [Local Cant, U. S.]
To sleep beyond; as, to oversleep one's self or one's usual hour of rising.
To sleep too long.
To slide over or by.
To slip or slide over; to pass easily or carelessly beyond; to omit; to neglect; as, to overslip time or opportunity.
An outer garment, or slop. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To render slow; to check; to curb. [Obs.] Hammond.
Too slow.
An overseer; a superintendent.
An umpire; a third arbiter, appointed when two arbiters, previously selected, disagree.
To cover with snow, or as with snow. [Poetic] Shak. Dryden.
Too soon. Sir P. Sidney.
To grieve or afflict to excess. [Obs.] Milton.
The all-containing soul. [R.] That unity, that oversout, within which every man's particular being is contained and made one with all other. Emerson.
To sow where something has already been sown. [R.] His enemy came and oversowed cockle among the wheat. Matt. x
To reach or extend over.
To exceed in speaking; to speak too much; to use too many words.
To spin out to too great length; to protract unduly. W. Cartwright.
To spread over; to cover; as, the deluge overspread the earth. Chaucer. Those nations of the North Which overspread the world. Drayton.
To be spread or scattered over.
To spring or leap over.
To stand on the price or conditions of, so as to lose a sale; to lose by an extravagant price or hard conditions. [Obs.] What madman would o'erstand his market twice Dryden.
To outstare. [Obs.] Shak.
To stare wildly. [Obs.] Ascham.
To state in too strong terms; to exaggerate. Fuller.
An exaggerated statement or account.
To stay beyond the time or the limits of; as, to overstay the appointed time. Bp. Hall.
To step over or beyond; to transgress. Shak.
Stock in excess. Tatler.
To fill too full; to supply in excess; as, to overstock a market with goods, or a farm with cattle.
To overstock. Sir. M. Hale.
The clearstory, or upper story, of a building.
To strain one's self to excess. Dryden.
To stretch or strain too much; as to overstrain one's nerves. Ayliffe.
Too straitly or strictly. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.
To overstrew. [Obs.] Shak.
To strew or scatter over.
Excessively strict.
To stride over or beyond.
To strike beyond. [Obs.]
See Overstrew.
Too studious.
Excessively subtile.
A sum or quantity over; surplus. [Obs.] Holinshed.
To supply in excess.
An excessive supply. A general oversupply or excess of all commodities. J. S. Mill.
Excessively sure.
To bear sway over.
To swell or rise above; to overflow. [R.] Shak.
Open to view; public; apparent; manifest. Overt and apparent virtues bring forth praise. Bacon.

Not covert; open; public; manifest; as, an overt act of treason. Macaulay. No person shall be convicted of treason unless on the testimony of two witnesses to the same overt act, or on confession in open court. Constitution of the U. S.

To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress, or motion; to catch up with. Follow after the men; and when thou dost overtake them, say . . . Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good. Gen. xliv. 4. He had him overtaken in his flight. Spenser.
To come upon from behind; to discover; to surprise; to capture; to overcome. If a man be overtaken in a fault. Gal. vi. 1 I shall see The winged vengeance overtake such children. Shak.
Hence, figuratively, in the past participle (overtaken), drunken. [Obs.] Holland.
To talk to excess. Milton.
To task too heavily.
To tax or to task too heavily.
Too tedious.
To tempt exceedingly, or beyond the power of resistance. Milton.

synonyms: demolish; overturn; prostrate; destroy; ruin; subvert; overcome; conquer; defeat; discomfit; vanquish; beat; rout.
definitions: To throw over; to overturn; to upset; to turn upside down. His wife overthrew the table. Jer. Taylor.
To cause to fall or to fail; to subvert; to defeat; to make a ruin of; to destroy. When the walls of Thebes he overthrew. Dryden. [Gloucester] that seeks to overthrow religion. Shak.
The act of overthrowing; the state of being overthrow; ruin. Your sudden overthrow much rueth me. Spenser.
Having a transverse position; placed or situated across; hence, opposite. "Our overthwart neighbors." Dryden.
Crossing in kind or disposition; perverse; adverse; opposing. "Overthwart humor." Clarendon.
Across; crosswise; transversely. "Y'clenched overthwart and endelong." Chaucer.
Across; from alde to side of. "Huge trees overthwart one another." Milton.
That which is overthwart; an adverse circumstance; opposition. [Obs.] Surrey.
To cross; to oppose. [Obs.]
In an overthwart manner;across; also, perversely. [Obs.] Peacham.
The state of being overthwart; perverseness. [Obs.] Lord Herbert.
To tilt over; to overturn.
Time beyond, or in excess of, a limit; esp., extra working time.
To tire to excess; to exhaust.
To become too tired. Br. Hall.
To give too high a title to.
Publicly; openly.
To overwork.
To weary excessively; to exhaust. Then dozed a while herself, but overtoiled By that day's grief and travel. Tennyson.
